query: For high-entropy alloys intended for thermal-insulation or radiation-resistant applications, what single intervention could reduce phonon thermal conductivity? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the physical mechanism, the predicted change relative to an otherwise comparable untreated alloy, the temperature and material-state boundaries over which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing lattice defects through 3D ink-extrusion printing can reduce phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys
generation.falsification_experiment: Measure thermal conductivity of 3D ink-extrusion printed high-entropy alloys and compare to untreated alloys

3D Ink‐Extrusion Printing

The 3D ink extrusion printing, sintering, and silicide coating processes are shown in Figure 1 a . The ≈410 µm filaments containing metallic/hydride powders are printed layer by layer to produce complex parts, including a lattice sandwich structure, as shown in Figure 1b . When the filaments are extruded, the solvent (dichloromethane, DCM) evaporates near‐instantaneously, and the binder (polystyrene, PS) precipitates, leading to a quick increase in the strength of filaments that helps the structure to self‐support. After sintering, these samples are nearly fully densified and show neither cracking nor warpage. After a subsequent silicide coating, the oxidation resistance of the 3D‐printed part is very significantly improved, which is a key step to making 3D‐printed RHEA structures useful at high temperatures.

a) Schematic illustration of 3D ink extrusion printing, sintering, and silicide coating of a lattice‐core sandwich; oxidation mechanisms are also shown. b) Photographs of 3D ink extrusion printed, sintered, and silicide‐coated lattice‐core sandwich.
